updates.title: Software {{version}}, {{count}} updates available
updates.meta: This box maintains itself: the operating system and its packages, the packages Vedette pins, and Vedette itself. Software updates come only from signed GitHub releases; the box refuses packages that are unsigned or badly signed.

channelHint.stable: Builds that ran at least 7 days on beta first. Recommended.
channelHint.beta: Get new builds early; they may have bugs. Use on a test box only.

modeHint.auto: The box installs new builds when a check finds them. Boxes get them in waves to limit risk.

updates.checkOff: Update checks are off in Privacy.

sources.body: Software updates come only from signed GitHub releases. Feeds (CISA KEV, FIRST EPSS, NVD, vendor advisories, IOC feeds and your own) are fetched by the box directly from each source, never through GitHub. Confirmed recommendation packs ship inside updates.

managed.desc: Tools Vedette installs and pins itself. They are not taken from the operating system's package mirrors.
managed.pending: New version in the next release

vedette.title: Vedette software
vedette.desc: Signed releases from GitHub, with a spare slot and a one-click rollback. Channel and history are here.

os.title: Operating system of this box
os.desc: This box is a security appliance, so it keeps its own operating system patched. Ubuntu and Debian are supported.
os.noCheckYet: The box has not looked for operating system updates yet. Click Check now.

supHint.ended: This release no longer gets security fixes. Upgrade the release below as soon as you can.

os.autoHintOff: Nothing is installed until you press a button below. Security fixes can wait for days.

window.title: Maintenance window
window.hintAnytime: Automatic Vedette updates and scheduled reboots can happen at any time of day.

os.installAllBody: This installs security and normal updates. Services may restart for a few seconds. A database backup is taken first.
os.helper: A separate privileged helper, vedette-host, runs a fixed list of apt commands. The web app never runs shell commands. A database backup is taken before every run, and only one run can go at a time.
os.pendingEmpty: Nothing waiting. The operating system is up to date.

privacy.title: The box connects out only for the flows listed below
privacy.meta: Assets, logs, findings and AI keys never leave the machine. Below is every data flow that goes out to the Internet.
privacy.flows: Data flows that leave the box
privacy.flowsDesc: A flow that only runs when you configure it says so. There is no other flow. Reporting a problem is not a flow: the box sends nothing, and your own browser opens GitHub.

1.name: Pull feeds directly from their sources
1.what: The box fetches each feed itself with plain HTTPS requests for public files. None of your data is sent; only your IP address appears in the source's logs. Vedette's own GitHub repository is used only for software updates; some public sources happen to host their files on GitHub.
1.to: CISA KEV (www.cisa.gov; if that address answers 403, an error or nothing in time, CISA's own GitHub mirror of the same file on raw.githubusercontent.com), FIRST EPSS (api.first.org), the affected versions of the exploited CVEs from the NVD (services.nvd.nist.gov: each request carries only fixed parameters, the record number it starts at and, after the first day, the date window of the change, with the same Vedette User-Agent as every feed), the nuclei-templates CVE list, IPsum and hagezi TIF (public data files on raw.githubusercontent.com), ET Open (rules.emergingthreats.net), abuse.ch Feodo Tracker (feodotracker.abuse.ch), the Tor exit list (check.torproject.org), and any custom feed you add
1.control: Cannot be turned off as a whole because the product needs this data; you can turn off a built-in feed such as the NVD versions (no more requests; the versions already loaded are still used, without updates), and remove a custom feed to stop it.
1.customNone: You have no feed of your own turned on.

2.name: Anonymous signal
2.what: Not sent. The box sends nothing to the Vedette project. The project runs no server that could receive it.

3.name: AI assistant
3.what: The data you choose to send (findings, the log summary) to your provider with your key, job by job:
items: Test (a profile): three tiny fixed requests (a one-word prompt, then the same with a dummy tool and with a JSON format, to learn what the model supports) with that profile's key to its address; no data of yours is in them, and each test is written to the audit log (never the key).

Model list (the Add AI profile dialog, D-475): one GET of the provider's model endpoint (for example /v1/models) with that profile's key, to show the models to pick from; no data of yours is in it, only the key as the provider's own header. The box asks, not your browser, through the same guarded connection as every AI call (no redirects; Vedette itself and forbidden addresses are refused at connect time, except that through a proxy you configure for cloud profiles the proxy makes the connection), keeps only clean model names, and writes the call to the audit log with the host (never the key).

Explain (a CVE or a finding): the public exploited-list entry (CVE text, vendor, product, links) and, for each device it matches, the device name, IP address, kind, how it was matched (by version or by product) and the finding status, to the profile assigned to that job.

Finding brief (the AI button of a finding, and the draft of a recommendation): the same entry plus, for that one device, its display name, the finding's severity and confidence, and whether a confirmed recommendation pack exists.

Response plan (only once an administrator assigns a profile to it; it then runs by itself every 5 minutes, at most 20 calls a day, and does nothing while AI proposals are paused): for each open critical finding that has no plan yet, the CVE id and its public exploited-list entry, the device name, IP address and kind, and the list of response actions the AI may propose (their names, descriptions, risk and parameter names, never commands, paths or credentials; for an action on a device, the id of the connection it runs through), and the reads the box itself made through those connections in the last 24 hours (for each: an id, the connection id and name, the read tool's name and the time, never what the read returned), to that profile.

Personal data: before sending, the personal-data hook masks email addresses, phone numbers and device secrets (passwords, password hashes, SNMP communities, pre-shared and private keys written in configurations, log lines and the output of read tools) and stops the call when the text holds an ID number, unless an administrator turns off Block personal data (Settings → AI assistant, or the Hooks tab), and the answer is checked again by the hooks.

Log summary (the Regenerate now button of the AI log digest on the Logs page): from the last 24 hours of logs, only the kinds of log line (the line with its variable parts removed) with their source name and counts, the kinds far above their usual rate, and each connection to an address a threat feed lists (the device name, its IP address, the address it contacted, how it was seen, whether the device that logged it blocked it, the names of the feeds and a confidence), never a log line, to the profile assigned to that job.

Log investigation (at the maximum level, when it has a profile): that profile receives the same summary and may ask, through read-only tools, for what the logs counted about one IP address in a window of the last 24 hours (the kinds of log line that named it as the remote side, with their source name and counts, and its connections to addresses a threat feed lists, blocked or not; never a log line) and for the same device, indicator and exploited-list results as Ask your data (below).

Suggested memories: when an administrator lets the AI suggest new memories, its answer may carry up to two, which stay on the box until an administrator accepts or rejects them; with the privacy rule on only a profile inside your network receives it, and the same masking and hooks apply.
Company rules an administrator writes (up to 30, each up to 300 characters) are sent to the provider with every call, as part of the instructions.

Memories an administrator keeps (up to 100, each up to 300 characters; only the ones switched on, never a suggestion nobody accepted) are sent with every call that carries internal data, as fenced data the model is told never to obey, after the same masking and hooks as the rest; calls on public text only (CVE news, advisory translation) do not carry them.

CVE news: the public exploited-list entry and the public text the box fetched for that CVE (flow 8: the NVD record, a vendor advisory, the GitHub repositories that name it, and blog posts that mention it), cleaned and capped, and nothing of your network.

Documents an administrator adds to the knowledge base (PDF, MD, TXT or DOCX, up to 10 MB and 50 documents) are read and indexed on the box, and adding or indexing a document sends nothing anywhere; only the text kept from them, never the file, is stored. When a call is made for a job the document is assigned to, and the job carries internal data (not CVE news or advisory translation), the few passages of the text that match the question (up to 4 passages, 12,000 characters in all) are sent with that call, as fenced data the model is told never to obey, after the same masking and hooks, passage by passage, as the memories.

Ask your data (a question an operator types on the AI assistant page): the question and then, in answer to what the model asks for, the results of read-only tools: devices of the inventory (name, IP address, kind, vendor, model, operating system, open ports, software, whether approved, when it was first and last seen, whether it was found on the network or added by hand, and which source saw it; never its notes), findings (device name and IP, CVE, status, severity, scan evidence summary), the exploited-list entry of a CVE with the devices it matches, whether a feed lists an IP address or a domain the model names, and the text a read tool of a connection you enabled returns from that device or server (never its credential). Each result is capped (4 KB a call, 12 KB a question, 8 calls; a list sends its counts and its first 10 rows), goes through the same masking and hooks as the question, result by result, and is sent as fenced data the model is told never to obey; a result a hook stops is not sent. When the privacy rule is on, only a profile inside your network receives these results.

Arguments of read tools: for a read tool of a connection the AI writes the arguments itself; they can contain data the AI saw from the box (masked by the personal-data hook, and checked by your before-tool hooks first), and they are sent to that connection. While the privacy rule is on, only tools of connections whose address is inside your network are offered.

Every call: text from feeds and from devices is sent only as fenced data the model is told never to obey. Every call is written to the AI activity log as hashes only: the text sent and received is not stored. A profile marked as inside your network must use a private address or a name that resolves to one; this is checked at every connection.
3.to: The AI providers you add (one or more profiles), or a model inside your network
3.control: No AI profile, no flow. You choose which profile handles each job and can keep logs and device data on profiles inside your network.

4.name: Data sources that need a key
4.what: IP, domain and hash lookups to services you gave a key for.

5.name: Notifications
5.what: Alert content, the 6-digit sign-in code for people who use two-step email codes, and a 6-digit link code that proves an approver's email address (mailed to that address); for Telegram and Zalo personal, a confirm link to this box with the Vedette user's name, sent privately by the Telegram bot (if it may not write to them yet, a note without the link asks them in the approval chat to press Start) or by the box's Zalo account to the approver's account, which they open and confirm while signed in to Vedette. Email goes through the SMTP server you set: your own, or a provider you choose under your account (Gmail, SendGrid, Microsoft 365, Outlook.com at smtp-mail.outlook.com and others). OAuth sign-ins add a token service, contacted only with those presets: login.microsoftonline.com for Microsoft 365 and Outlook.com, oauth2.googleapis.com for Google Workspace and Gmail with your own Google client. As an app, Microsoft 365 gets a token with the tenant ID, client ID and client secret; Google Workspace with a request signed with the service account key, naming the mailbox (the key never leaves the box). With a user sign-in (Microsoft 365 or Outlook.com by device code, Gmail with your own Google OAuth client) the box gets a device code and then tokens from login.microsoftonline.com, or exchanges the code from the address you paste at oauth2.googleapis.com; it keeps the refresh token encrypted and the mailbox's address, and refreshes the access token there before sending. Access tokens stay in memory only. Zalo OA with a refresh token: before the access token ends (about 25 hours) the box sends the refresh token, your Zalo app's App ID and Secret key to oauth.zaloapp.com and keeps the new refresh token Zalo sends back, encrypted; alerts go to openapi.zalo.me. Slack: Incoming Webhook, plus an outward Socket Mode connection if you approve actions in Slack. Telegram: bot with long polling; once a request is decided or has ended, the box edits its approval message to remove the buttons. Zalo personal (unofficial): an administrator signs in with a QR code (the box talks to id.zalo.me, chat.zalo.me and jr.chat.zalo.me for that), and to pick the recipient and approvers the box asks Zalo for the account's friends and groups, the group of an invite link you paste or the person of a phone number you type; the box then signs in to Zalo with that account's session and sends alerts, and approval codes privately to each approver's own Zalo user ID; it reads the direct messages to that account to take approvers' reply codes, answers them privately, and notes the Zalo user ID and name of any other sender in the audit log. Email approvals add a single-use link valid for 30 minutes that opens a confirmation page on this box. Approval requests sent to Telegram, Slack, Zalo and email carry the whole change: the full command or API call with its non-credential header values and body, the undo and the check before. The response action webhook_call, if an administrator adds it to a rule, posts the request id, the item id and the action text to the webhook you configured.
5.to: The Slack, Telegram, Zalo OA, Zalo personal or webhook you set up, or the SMTP server you set for email (such as smtp-mail.outlook.com for Outlook.com), plus login.microsoftonline.com (Microsoft 365, Outlook.com) or oauth2.googleapis.com (Google Workspace, Gmail with your own Google client) for OAuth sign-in tokens, and oauth.zaloapp.com for the Zalo OA access token
5.control: Remove the channel, or turn off approvals in chat, to stop it (buttons already sent are still removed while the channel exists).

6.name: Update checks
6.what: Your current Vedette version (in the request to GitHub). For the operating system (D-53) the box runs `apt` through the privileged helper `vedette-host`, and the request carries what any apt client sends: the release and architecture of this machine and the package names it asks about. To install an update, the same helper pulls the container images of the Vedette release by digest, and the request carries what any container client sends: the image name and digest and the architecture of this machine. `vedette-host` also builds the `scan` image on the box from the signed base image (D-113 (7), D-147), at install on every box (whether or not active scanning is turned on) and again whenever the `scan` image is pulled or updated: a build container, run with the network, installs nmap from the Debian package repository, and that request carries what any apt client sends (the release and architecture of the base image and the package name `nmap`). No Vedette data, no inventory, no findings
6.to: GitHub releases (signed software updates and the package of the system helper `vedette-host`; confirmed recommendation packs ship inside them; a release file download is redirected to a GitHub-owned file host, `objects.githubusercontent.com` or `release-assets.githubusercontent.com`), ghcr.io (the signed container images of a release, pulled by digest) with the host it redirects to for the image layers, pkg-containers.githubusercontent.com, and the distribution's package mirrors: Ubuntu `archive.ubuntu.com` and `security.ubuntu.com`, Debian `deb.debian.org` and `security.debian.org`. You can point apt at a local mirror inside your network (edit the apt sources on the box; the mirror host list in Settings → Updates follows), so nothing leaves the network. The `scan` image build is the exception: it contacts Debian's `deb.debian.org` from inside the build container, also on an Ubuntu box, and the local mirror you gave apt on the box does not apply to it (the container has its own apt configuration)
6.control: Yes — switch update checks off to update by hand only. Operating system updates that you start yourself, or that unattended-upgrades installs, still contact the mirrors unless apt points at a local mirror, and an update you install by hand from the registry still contacts `ghcr.io` and GitHub releases (the system helper package). There is no setting that skips the `scan` image build at install or when the image is pulled. A box that cannot reach `deb.debian.org` installs without active scanning (core, sensor and honeypot still install) and tries the build again the next time the `scan` image is pulled; switching update checks off stops the later updates, not the build at install

container.what: Your current Vedette version (in the request to GitHub): the box downloads the signed release index, the manifest of the release it runs (once per version) and, when a newer release is offered to it, that release's manifest. Nothing else: a container-only install has no `vedette-host`, so the box runs no `apt`, pulls no image and builds no `scan` image. The `pull` you run yourself from Settings → Updates goes from your machine to `ghcr.io`, as any container client does. No Vedette data, no inventory, no findings
container.to: GitHub releases (signed software updates; confirmed recommendation packs ship inside them; a release file download is redirected to a GitHub-owned file host, `objects.githubusercontent.com` or `release-assets.githubusercontent.com`)
container.control: Yes — switch update checks off; Settings → Updates then cannot tell you when a release is out. A `pull` you run yourself still contacts `ghcr.io` and the host it redirects to for the image layers, `pkg-containers.githubusercontent.com`

7.name: Forwarding to a SIEM
7.what: The Vedette events you choose (findings, incidents, trap touches, connections to known-bad addresses) as syslog, CEF or JSON. Each record has the event name, time, severity, identifiers, addresses and short labels from the event; no log lines.
7.to: The SIEM or webhook target you enter
7.control: No configuration, no flow. Remove the target to turn it off.

8.name: News about a CVE
8.what: The CVE ID in two lookups (the NVD record and a GitHub repository search) and, when the CVE links to one of 16 listed vendor sites, a request for that advisory page; six security-blog feeds are fetched whole, with nothing of yours in the request. Links to other sites are shown, never fetched. Nothing of your network is in any request. Runs only when you press the button, part of the AI assistant module.
8.control: If you do not press it, nothing is sent. Turn off the AI assistant module to remove it.

9.name: External exposure
9.what: Your verified domain names, to find subdomains in public certificate-transparency logs: one search at crt.sh when you scan a domain. The scan itself goes only to your own verified targets: ports only on this box's verified public IPs, and one web-page check by name on ports 80 and 443 for the names of your domain. It sends nothing else of yours. And HTTPS requests to public "what is my IP" services so the box can see its own public IP. The services see only that IP; the requests carry no product name or identifier. An IP counts only when at least two of the three agree. The first check after install is a full check of 15 requests. Then auto-detect (on by default) asks each service once every recheck interval (60 minutes by default, 1 minute to 24 hours). A full check also runs at most once an hour by itself, when you select Detect now, when you turn auto-detect on, when you verify a public IP again, and just before a scan of a public IP (at most one every 5 minutes).
9.to: crt.sh (certificate-transparency search, run by Sectigo); your own targets when you scan; checkip.amazonaws.com (AWS), icanhazip.com (Cloudflare), ifconfig.me/ip (Google Cloud). No Vedette-run server
9.control: Turn off auto-detect under External exposure (then it is sent only when you select Detect now), or turn off the External exposure module.

10.name: Time sync (NTP)
10.what: A time request (UDP port 123) so the box clock stays right. No Vedette data is in it; the server only sees the box's IP address.
10.to: The time sources of your distribution's own chrony configuration, which the installer leaves as it finds it (D-166): Ubuntu 24.04 `ntp.ubuntu.com` and the `0-2.ubuntu.pool.ntp.org` pools (in `/etc/chrony/chrony.conf`); Ubuntu 26.04 the NTS servers `1-4.ntp.ubuntu.com` and `ntp-bootstrap.ubuntu.com` (in `/etc/chrony/sources.d/`); Debian 13 `2.debian.pool.ntp.org` (in `/etc/chrony/chrony.conf`); read the files on your box for the exact list. Also any NTP servers your DHCP server hands out (`/run/chrony-dhcp`). Once Settings → Box network is saved, the servers you enter there (they can be inside your network) are added to those, and if you save it with no NTP server, `pool.ntp.org` is added
10.control: Not from Vedette's screens: the operating system's own time sources stay. To send nothing outside, point the box's chrony at a server inside your network yourself (see the runbook).

container.what: Nothing from Vedette. A container-only install sets no time source: the containers keep the clock of the machine that runs them
container.to: Nowhere from Vedette. The time service of the machine that runs the containers (set up by you or its operating system) is outside Vedette
container.control: Not sent by Vedette. Keep the clock of that machine right (Linux: systemd-timesyncd or chrony; macOS and Windows set it by themselves): sign-in codes, certificates and the update check need a correct clock

11.name: Single sign-on (OIDC)
11.what: Only if you set up SSO: the box reads the discovery document and the signing keys from the issuer address you entered, and exchanges the one-time sign-in code for a token. It sends your client ID and client secret, the one-time code and the PKCE verifier; the identity provider sees the box's IP address and its redirect address. The person's browser goes to the identity provider to sign in and comes back to the box. The box keeps no token from the identity provider. No devices, findings, logs or AI data are sent.
11.to: The identity provider whose issuer address you entered (it can be inside your network)
11.control: Turn off the SSO module (auth-oidc). Password sign-in keeps working.

12.name: Connections you add
12.what: The requests and actions you set up are sent to the connection's own address, which you typed (a public address is allowed; you type it on purpose). The credentials you entered (token, or user name and password) go there too (a token goes as Authorization: Bearer, or in the header you name for it); an SSH key is used to sign in but not sent. Nothing else is added, nothing goes to any other host, and the device sees the box's IP address. Sent when you press Test on a connection that is on, when an approved action or its undo runs, and when the AI uses an allowed read tool. For a read tool the AI writes the arguments itself: they can contain data the AI saw from the box (masked first) and they are sent to that connection, even at a public address; while the privacy rule is on, only tools of connections inside your network are offered. The AI can use only read tools on the allow-list; a write tool runs only through an action a person approves.
12.to: Only the address you typed for each connection
12.control: Delete the connection, or turn it off. Nothing is sent to a connection that is off.

13.name: MCP server, read by tools you connect
13.what: Only while you turn on the MCP server. The box sends nothing by itself: an AI tool or SIEM you give a token to asks, and gets the devices, findings and vulnerability-feed entries its token's scopes allow. No passwords, keys, tokens, users, audit log, log lines, AI history or settings are ever in an answer. The box listens on this machine only (localhost); a tool on another machine reaches it only through a tunnel or proxy you set up. What the tool does with the answers, for example sending them to its own AI provider, is up to that tool.
13.to: Only the tools you gave a token to, through this machine
13.control: Revoke the token, or turn off the MCP server. Tokens stop working at once.

14.name: Wazuh pull (only if you connect it)
14.what: Only while a Wazuh server is connected in Inventory → Agents and the agent intake module is on. The box signs in to the Wazuh server API address you typed with the read-only user name and password you entered, then only reads: the API version, the list of agents, and each agent's network addresses, network interfaces and installed packages. It sends nothing else and never changes anything in Wazuh. The certificate must be one a public authority vouches for, or the one pinned when you pressed Save; if it changes, the pull stops before the password is sent, and you trust the new one only by typing the password again and pressing Save. Sent when you press Test or Save, and at the interval you chose.
14.to: Only the Wazuh server address you typed
14.control: Disconnect Wazuh in Inventory → Agents (the saved password is deleted), or turn off the agent intake module.

telemetry.title: Anonymous signal
telemetry.statement: Anonymous signal: not sent. The box sends nothing to the Vedette project. The project runs no server that could receive it, and this version has no code that sends it.

cookie.title: Cookies
cookie.body: One sign-in session cookie only (__Host-vedette_session). No tracking, no analytics, no resources loaded from outside servers.

bugNote.title: Report a problem
bugNote.body: The box sends nothing when you report a problem. You download a filtered diagnostic file and press Open GitHub issue; your own browser opens GitHub with your text filled in.

mcp.titleOn: MCP server is on, read-only, {{count}} tokens
mcp.meta: Lets outside AI tools or a SIEM look up the box's devices, findings and vulnerability feeds. Read-only; there are no write tools.
mcp.disabledToast: MCP server is off. Tokens are kept but do not work.
mcp.onHintContainer: Listening inside the vedette-core container. The compose.yaml of this release publishes it on the localhost of the machine that runs the container only.
mcp.offHint: No port is open. Turn it on to create tokens and connect.
mcp.connectDesc: Paste this config into your MCP tool and replace <token> with a token below.
mcp.bindNote: localhost only, not open to the network
mcp.remote: A tool on another machine must go through an SSH tunnel or a reverse proxy you set up. Vedette does not open this port to the LAN. Tools that run inside a web browser cannot connect: the server refuses requests from web pages.
mcp.remoteContainer: The compose.yaml of this release publishes the port on 127.0.0.1 of the machine that runs Docker or Podman, never on the LAN; with an older compose.yaml no tool can connect until you update it. A tool on another machine must go through an SSH tunnel to that machine or a reverse proxy you set up. Tools that run inside a web browser cannot connect: the server refuses requests from web pages.
mcp.notListening: The port is not open yet.
mcp.notListeningHint: Do not give a token to this address until the port is open: another program listening there would receive it.
mcp.verify: The format above follows the Claude Code MCP docs (type http, url, headers). Other tools may name the fields differently: check that tool's docs.

token.title: Read-only tokens
token.desc: One token per tool, with only the scope it needs. Revoke any time.
token.name: Token name
token.nameError: Name the token so you know which one to revoke later.
token.createdBody: Copy the token now: once you close this dialog it cannot be shown again. The box keeps only the last 4 characters.
token.label: Token
token.empty: No tokens yet. Create one so an outside tool can connect.

revokeAsk.title: Revoke token {{name}}?
revokeAsk.body: The tool that uses it loses access at once. This cannot be undone: to connect it again, create a new token.

tools.title: Tools the MCP server offers
tools.desc: All are read tools. None can edit devices, change a finding's status or run a scan.
tools.get_asset: Show one device and its software
tools.get_finding: Show one finding and its evidence
tools.lookup_cve: Look up a CVE in the exploited list
tools.lookup_ioc: Look up a bad IP or domain

data.title: Back up, export and delete the box's data
data.meta: All of this works from here, no command line. Your data stays on this machine.

backup.title: Backup
backup.desc: Settings, users (with their password hashes, never the passwords themselves), modules, devices, findings and the log. No AI keys or tokens. Keep the file as safe as the box: the hashes could be attacked offline.

restore.title: Backups on this box
restore.desc: Copies the operating system helper keeps on the box: the ones you made and the ones the box takes by itself before an operating system install, a Vedette update or a restore. Restoring one puts the box's data back to that moment.
restore.empty: No backups on this box yet.

ask.title: Restore the backup from {{when}}?
ask.lost: Everything written since then is replaced: devices, findings, alerts, logs, users and settings.
ask.kept: Before it restores, the box keeps a copy of the data it has now, listed here as Before restore, so you can go back.
ask.restart: Vedette restarts during the restore; this page reconnects by itself.
ask.understand: I understand that data written since this backup is replaced
ask.retention: The box keeps the last 3 Before restore copies.
ask.pushesOut: This restore adds one, so the oldest Before restore copy, from {{when}}, is deleted.

restore.running: Restoring the backup from {{when}}. Vedette is restarting; this page reconnects by itself.
restore.done: Restored the backup from {{when}}. The data from before the restore is kept as a backup.
restore.reverted: The restored data did not start correctly, so the box put back the data it had before. Nothing was lost.

export.title: Export data
export.desc: Every table of the box as JSON, to take to another tool: devices, findings, logs, settings and users with their names and email addresses. Passwords, keys, tokens and webhook addresses are never included (a webhook shows only its host).

purge.title: Delete all data
purge.desc: Deletes all data on this box: devices, findings, logs, users, settings, every module's data and every backup. The decryption key is replaced, so no old copy can be opened. The box restarts and returns to a fresh install. This cannot be undone.

ask.title: Delete all data on the box?
ask.body: Download an export first if you still need the data. You are signed out, the box restarts (the page is unreachable for a few seconds) and first-run setup opens again.
ask.removes: Deleted: all data, users and backups, including the data of every module. The decryption key is replaced.
ask.keeps: Kept: the TLS certificate, the system journal (the operating system rotates it; Vedette does not control it), the box's network settings and the honeypot's raw log (its container owns it).
ask.type: Type the organization name "{{org}}" to confirm
ask.codeApp: The 6-digit code from your authenticator app.
ask.codeEmail: Click Delete everything once to get a code by email, then type it here and click again.

done.title: All data deleted
done.body: The box is restarting and will open first-run setup. Not deleted:

kept.host_backups: Backups made by the operating system helper: this box is set up without the helper (container-only install: the helper's socket is turned off in its settings), so there were none to delete here. Check the host that runs the container for backups.
kept.honeypot_log: The honeypot's raw log on the box (the honeypot container owns it): its old lines are still in that file, but the fresh box does not read them again.
kept.key_not_replaced: The decryption key could not be replaced. Old copies of the data stay readable with it: replace the key file on the box by hand.

sample.title: Restore sample data
sample.desc: Trial build only: puts everything back to the original sample data, including anything you entered.

ask.title: Restore sample data?
ask.body: Everything you entered in this trial build is erased. The page reloads with the original sample data and signs you in again as the sample administrator.

logs.title: Download logs
logs.desc: One file with the box's logs. Secrets (passwords, keys, tokens, webhook addresses) are never included. Hash-chained logs include their hashes so you can verify them offline.
logs.range: The start date is after the end date.
logs.verify: Verify offline: hash = SHA-256(previous hash + the entry as JSON with sorted keys, without its hash).

account.title: {{name}}'s account
account.meta: Profile, password, two-step sign-in and the places you are signed in.

password.title: Change password
password.desc: At least {{min}} characters. A long sentence is easier to remember than random characters.
password.shortError: The new password needs at least {{min}} characters.
password.mismatch: The two entries do not match.

twofa.title: Two-step sign-in
twofa.desc: On top of your password, signing in needs a 6-digit code. Pick one method; to switch, turn it off and set up the other.
twofa.appActive: Signing in asks for the 6-digit code shown in your authenticator app.
twofa.emailActive: Signing in asks for a 6-digit code that Vedette emails to {{to}}.

app.desc: Google Authenticator, Microsoft Authenticator, Aegis or any app that supports time-based codes.
app.scan: Scan this QR code with your authenticator app, or enter the key by hand.
app.qrLabel: QR code for your authenticator app
app.enter: Then enter the 6-digit code the app shows to confirm.

email.desc: Vedette emails a 6-digit code to your sign-in address, {{to}}.
email.moduleOff: Email codes need the Notifications module, which is off.
email.notReady: Email codes need the email alert channel, which is not set up or is turned off.
email.askAdmin: Ask an administrator to set up the email channel.
email.sent: We sent a 6-digit code to {{to}}. Enter it to confirm that this mailbox works. The code expires in 10 minutes.
email.codeHint: The code can be used once. After 5 wrong tries it is cancelled and you need a new one.
email.resendIn: Send a new code in {{s}} s

twofa.startPasswordHint: Needed to turn on two-step sign-in, as it is to turn it off.
twofa.codeHint: The code changes every 30 seconds. If it is wrong, enter a fresh one.
twofa.lostUser: Lost your phone or mailbox? Ask an administrator to turn two-step sign-in off for you in Settings → Users.
twofa.lostAdmin: Lost your phone or mailbox? Another administrator can turn two-step sign-in off for you in Settings → Users. If you are the only one, run this on the machine that runs Vedette (on an appliance: sudo podman instead of docker). It gives a temporary password and turns two-step sign-in off.

offAsk.title: Turn off two-step sign-in?
offAsk.body: The account will be protected by the password alone.

guide.title: New to authenticator apps? We recommend Google Authenticator.
guide.install: Install Google Authenticator on your phone:
guide.scan: Open it, tap + and choose Scan a QR code, then point the camera at the code above.
guide.type: Type the 6-digit code the app shows into the box below. A new code appears every 30 seconds.
guide.other: Microsoft Authenticator, Aegis, 1Password or any app with time-based codes works the same way.

sessions.title: Where you are signed in
sessions.desc: If you see a session you do not know, end it and change your password.

sso.title: Password and two-step sign-in
sso.body: You sign in through your company account (SSO). Your password and two-step sign-in are set at your identity provider, not in Vedette. Your role comes from your groups there and is updated each time you sign in.

twoStepPrompt.title: Turn on two-step sign-in for this administrator account
twoStepPrompt.body: An administrator can change every setting of the box. With two-step sign-in, a password that leaks is not enough: signing in also needs a code from an authenticator app or an email.

alertChannelPrompt.title: No alert channel yet
alertChannelPrompt.body: Until an alert channel is set up and switched on, Vedette can only show what it finds here: nobody is told when a device matches an exploited vulnerability.
alertChannelPrompt.noAlerts: Not using alerts? Switch off Notifications in Settings, Modules, and this goes away.

changePassword.title: Choose a new password
changePassword.desc: An administrator set your current password. Choose your own before you continue: at least {{min}} characters, and not the temporary one.
changePassword.currentError: Enter the temporary password you signed in with.
changePassword.sameError: The new password must differ from the temporary one.

login.codeHint: This account has two-step sign-in. Get the code from your authenticator app.
login.codeHintEmail: We sent a 6-digit code to {{to}}. It expires in 10 minutes.
login.resendIn: Send a new code in {{s}} s
login.resent: A new code was sent to {{to}}.

setup.title: First-time Vedette setup
setup.subtitle: Three steps, a few minutes. You can change every step later in Settings, and set up alert channels there once setup is done.

account.title: Organization and administrator account
account.desc: This account is the first administrator, with full control over settings.
account.orgError: Enter the organization name (at least 2 characters).
account.name: Administrator name
account.emailError: The email does not look right, for example name@example.com.
account.passwordHint: At least {{min}} characters. A long sentence is easier to remember than random characters.
account.passwordError: The password needs at least {{min}} characters, it has {{count}} so far.
account.againError: The two entries do not match.
account.codeHint: Vedette prints a one-time code in its log each time it starts while setup is open. On the appliance run "journalctl -u vedette-core | grep setup_code"; on a container-only install run "docker logs vedette-core 2>&1 | grep setup_code" (or podman logs). Copy the code.
account.codeHintAppliance: Vedette prints a one-time code in its log each time it starts while setup is open. On the box run "journalctl -u vedette-core | grep setup_code" and copy the code.
account.codeHintContainer: Vedette prints a one-time code in its log each time it starts while setup is open. Run "docker logs vedette-core 2>&1 | grep setup_code" (or "podman logs vedette-core") on the machine that runs it, and copy the code.
account.codeError: Enter the setup code from the box's log.

network.title: Network to watch
network.desc: Vedette listens and (if you confirm) scans only inside these ranges.
network.lanHint: One range per row, like 192.168.10.0/24. Write the prefix length too: a bare address such as 192.168.10.0 is refused. Printers and cameras should be inside the list.
network.lanFromBox: The first row is the box's own network ({{lan}}); change it or add others.
network.lanBlank: Fill in this range or remove the row.
network.lanBad: "{{value}}" is not a valid range. Write it like 192.168.10.0/24 (address, slash, prefix length 0 to 32).
network.lanPublic: {{value}} is not a private range (10.x, 172.16-31.x, 192.168.x, 100.64-127.x). Add public addresses later under External exposure.
network.lanDup: {{value}} is listed twice. Remove one of the rows.
network.lanMany: At most 16 ranges. Merge them into larger ranges.

note.prefix: "{{from}}" had no prefix length, so it was read as {{to}} (a /24 holds 254 addresses). Change it if your network is a different size.
note.network: "{{from}}" was changed to {{to}}, the first address of that range.

network.commitment: I confirm these ranges belong to my company and I am allowed to scan them.
network.passiveOnly: Not ticked: Vedette only listens passively and does not scan yet. You can confirm later under Devices, Scope and sensors.
network.firstPass: Ticked: active scanning is turned on. Vedette makes one first pass over these ranges right away (once, at most an hour), then scans only in the time window under Devices, Scope and sensors (22:00 to 05:00 by default).
network.license: Vedette is provided as is under the Apache-2.0 license; its author, Kien Nguyen, is not responsible for how you use it.
network.saveFailed: Setup finished but the scan scope was not saved: {{message}} Open Devices, Scope and sensors to enter it again.
network.lanNoPrefix: "{{value}}" has no prefix length. Add it so Vedette scans the right size of network, for example {{value}}/24 or {{value}}/25.

modules.title: Choose a module bundle
modules.desc: Modules are separate pieces of work you switch on and off. Pick the closest bundle and change it later in Settings, Modules.

smb.name: Small business
smb.desc: Know your devices, see exploited vulnerabilities that match them, alert through a channel, internal traps, weekly report. Light, little upkeep.
smb.descNoTraps: Know your devices, see exploited vulnerabilities that match them, alert through a channel, weekly report. Light, little upkeep.

mid.name: Mid-size business
mid.desc: The small bundle plus confirming scans, external surface, firewall logs and the AI assistant (with your own key).

custom.name: Custom
custom.desc: Pick each module yourself. A module that needs another gets it picked too.

modules.pickHint: Core is always on. Picking a module that needs others picks them too; dropping a module also drops those that depend on it.
modules.notHere: Not on this install: {{list}}. They need the appliance install (vedette-host); this container-only install leaves them out.

sample.title: Just want a look?
sample.desc: Use sample data: 30 made-up devices, a few findings, and you are signed in at once as the sample administrator. Restore or delete it in Settings, Data.

preview.emailCode: Preview build: the email would contain {{code}}

bug.title: Report a problem
bug.desc: Describe what went wrong. You review everything before it leaves your hands.
bug.noSend: The box sends nothing itself. "Download report" saves a file on your computer, and "Open GitHub issue" opens GitHub in your own browser with the text below filled in. You decide what to post.
bug.bundleDesc: Exactly what the downloaded file contains besides your text. It never includes devices, logs, findings, keys, email addresses or IP addresses; those are removed from error messages.
bug.bundleLabel: JSON, preview of the diagnostic bundle
bug.attach: The GitHub issue holds your text and a short summary only. Attach the downloaded file to it so the maintainer can see the full bundle.

network.meta: Where the box sits on your network and how it listens to a switch mirror.
network.metaNoSpan: Where the box sits on your network: its ports, management address, decoy addresses and time source.
network.helper: Changes here are applied by vedette-host, a small helper on the box that runs a fixed list of commands. The web app never runs shell commands.

interfaces.title: Interfaces
interfaces.desc: The network ports of the box and what each one is used for.
interfaces.caption: Network interfaces of the box
interfaces.mgmtLocked: This is the port you reach this page through. Change its address under Management interface.

management.title: Management interface
management.desc: The address you use to open Vedette and the box's route to the rest of the network.
management.mode: How the box gets its address
management.dhcpNote: The address, gateway and DNS come from your DHCP server. Reserve the address on the server so it does not change.
management.dnsHint: One to three addresses, separated by commas.
management.pendingSaved: Applied. Confirm the new address in time or the box goes back to the old one.
management.revertedNow: The box went back to the old settings.

confirm.title: Change the management address?
confirm.body: You will lose this page. Open https://{{ip}}:8443 within 5 minutes and confirm, or the box returns to the old settings.
confirm.lose: If the new address is wrong or unreachable from your computer, do nothing: after 5 minutes the box goes back to the old address by itself.
confirm.signIn: You will need to sign in again at the new address (two-step code included): it is a different address for your browser.
confirm.bodyDhcp: You will lose this page. Your DHCP server picks the new address: find it there (or in your router's client list), open it on port 8443 within 5 minutes and confirm, or the box returns to the old settings.
confirm.loseDhcp: If you cannot find the new address, do nothing: after 5 minutes the box goes back to the old address by itself.

pending.body: Open https://{{ip}}:8443 and press Confirm there. If you do not, the box returns to {{old}}.
pending.confirm: Confirm: I opened the new address

span.title: SPAN capture
span.desc: Your switch sends a copy of the traffic of other ports to one port of the box. Vedette only listens: it never sends on that port and never blocks traffic.
span.portHint: The port the switch's mirror (SPAN) port is plugged into. It has no IP address and only listens. The management port cannot be used.

extractHint.dns: The names devices look up, to spot lookups of known-bad domains.
extractHint.tls_sni: The server name a device asks for when it starts an encrypted connection (the name only, not the content).
extractHint.http_host: The Host header of plain HTTP requests.
extractHint.flows: Who talked to whom: addresses, ports, byte counts and times.

span.readingNone: Nothing selected. SPAN cannot be turned on until you choose at least one.
span.filtersDesc: Traffic matching these is dropped before anything is read, for example a backup server or a port you do not want looked at.

cidr.label: Network range
cidr.hint: With the prefix length, for example 10.0.5.0/24.

host.label: Host
host.hint: An IPv4 address or a name, for example backup.lan.

port.label: Port number
port.hint: A number from 1 to 65535, for example 5353.

span.cpuHint: 5 to 50. Capture slows down instead of using more.
span.statusNote: The status shows the saved settings and refreshes every 5 seconds.
span.kept: This version of Vedette no longer sets up SPAN capture. What this box already has keeps working as saved and is shown here read-only: you can turn it off, not on again.

off.title: SPAN is off
off.advice: Turn on Capture mirrored traffic and choose the port to start listening.

ok.title: Receiving mirrored traffic
ok.advice: Packets from other devices are arriving on {{iface}}. The mirror works.

own_only.title: Only the box's own traffic
own_only.advice: Packets arrive on {{iface}} but none come from other devices. The switch is not mirroring other ports: check that the mirror session lists the ports you want to watch and that its destination is the port plugged into {{iface}}.

no_traffic.title: Nothing is arriving
no_traffic.advice: The link is up on {{iface}} but no packets arrive. Check the mirror session on the switch: is it enabled, is the destination the right port, and is the cable in that port?

sensor_unreachable.title: The listener did not start
sensor_unreachable.advice: Vedette saved the port but could not tell the passive sensor to listen on {{iface}}. It tries again every few seconds; if this stays, turn the passive sensor module off and on in Settings, Modules.

no_link.title: No cable signal
no_link.advice: {{iface}} has no link. Check the cable and that the switch port is on. A port set as a mirror destination must be enabled.

guides.title: Set up the mirror on your switch
guides.desc: Pick your switch to see the steps. Plug the switch's mirror destination port into {{port}} on the box.
guides.prompt: Choose a switch above to see the exact steps and commands.
guides.replace: Port names and numbers are examples. Replace them: the destination is the port plugged into {{port}}, the sources are the ports whose traffic you want to see.

check.partial: Partly verified, test on your model

guides.after: After the switch is set up, open SPAN capture above and check that {{port}} shows traffic from other devices.

decoys.title: Decoy addresses
decoys.desc: Extra IP addresses the box answers on for the traps, besides its own. Read only here.

ntp.title: Time (NTP)
ntp.desc: Where the box gets the time. Correct time matters for logs and certificates.
ntp.defaultNote: The box uses the time sources its operating system already has. Once you save Box network with Default, the box also asks the public {{pool}}.
ntp.serversHint: One to four names or addresses, separated by commas. They are added to the time sources the operating system already uses; those stay.
ntp.privacy: The operating system keeps its own time sources, so time requests still reach public servers (they see the box's IP address). Servers you enter here are added, not substituted.

boxAddress.title: Box address
boxAddress.desc: The name or address people and devices on your network use to reach the box. Every link the box sends uses it: alert messages, approval links, sign-in emails, the block list URL, URL honey tokens and agent install commands.
boxAddress.label: Host name or IP address
boxAddress.hint: Leave it empty to use the management address. Enter a name only if your network's DNS resolves it to the box. No https:// and no port.
boxAddress.noDefault: Default: the management address, once the box has one
boxAddress.noLinks: The box knows no address yet, so messages carry no links and approval requests cannot be sent.
boxAddress.saved: Box address saved. The certificate will include it within a few seconds.
boxAddress.savedOwnCert: Box address saved. Your own certificate must include it, or browsers and agents will warn.
boxAddress.reset: Box address set back to the management address.
boxAddress.previousLabel: Earlier box addresses still answered to
boxAddress.previous: Also still answering to {{address}} (agents, firewalls and links set up with it).
boxAddress.forgotten: The box no longer answers to {{address}}.

confirm.title: Change the box address?
confirm.body: Links, install commands and the block list URL will use {{to}} instead of {{from}}.
confirm.bodyDefault: Links, install commands and the block list URL will use the management address {{def}} instead of {{from}}.
confirm.keeps: Agents enrolled with {{from}}, firewalls that pull the block list from it and links already sent keep working: the box also keeps answering to {{from}} until you stop it here.

connections.title: Connections
connections.writeNoteLead: Write tools never run from a chat answer.
connections.writeNote: Tools that change something are used only through actions you approve in the AI response module.
connections.getMayChange: Some devices change state on a GET (reboot, config). Turn this on only for read-only endpoints.
connections.writeOnlyApproved: Write tools run only through an action you approve in the AI response module.
connections.emptyBody: Add a connection so response actions can reach a firewall or switch, and the AI can read a device instead of guessing.
connections.deleteBody: Response actions and the AI lose access to this system. Actions that used it can no longer run.
connections.dialogBody: The secret is stored encrypted on this box and used only to sign in to the address below.
connections.errAllow: Add at least one allow-list entry, one per line.

f.name: Name
f.target_mcp-stdio: Command that starts the MCP server
f.authHint: Changing it clears the secret you typed (a password is not a token); the user name and the other fields stay.
f.secretHint: Token, password or key. Stored encrypted; only the last 4 characters are shown afterwards.
f.secretSaved: Saved, ending {{last4}}. Leave blank to keep it.
f.allowHint_ssh: Exact commands the AI may run. Use a read-only device account.
f.allowHint_http: URL prefixes under the base address, for example {{example}}
f.allowHint_mcp-http: URL prefixes under the server address, for example {{example}}
f.allowHint_netconf-restconf: URL prefixes under the device address, for example {{example}}
f.allowHint_automation: URL prefixes under the platform address, for example {{example}}
f.usernameHintSsh: The account the box signs in with on the device.
f.usernameHintBasic: Sent with the password. It is not a secret.
f.authHeaderHint: Leave empty to send Authorization: Bearer
f.pinRoots: Trusted through a public certificate authority
f.pinNone: Nothing pinned yet. The first test trusts whatever answers at this address and pins it. Compare the fingerprint with the one the device shows. A device that a public certificate authority vouches for is not pinned by its key: from then on every test requires that trust.
f.forgetHint: The next test trusts whatever answers at this address and pins it. Compare the fingerprint with the one the device shows. Do this only when you know the device changed its certificate or key.
f.privateKey: Private key (OpenSSH or PEM, no passphrase)
f.keyHint: Paste the whole key, including the BEGIN and END lines. A key protected by a passphrase is refused. It is stored encrypted; afterwards only its fingerprint is shown.
f.keySaved: Saved, {{fingerprint}}. Leave blank to keep it.
f.keyKeep: Leave blank to keep the saved key
f.targetHint_automation: A platform such as Ansible AWX or n8n. For example {{example}}
f.targetHint_restconf: RESTCONF over HTTPS only. For example {{example}}

connections.meta: Devices and services that response actions and the AI reach: HTTP APIs, SSH or CLI, RESTCONF, automation platforms and MCP servers. Each connection only uses what is on its allow-list.
connections.privacyNote: Vedette sends requests only to the address you enter for each connection, when you press Test and when an approved action or an allowed read runs. The credentials you enter go to that address too. A public address is allowed when you add it on purpose.
connections.unsupportedBody: Vedette does not start an MCP server from a command. Delete this connection and add the server by its web address instead.
connections.pinLineRoots: Trusted through a public certificate authority since {{when}}. A certificate that no public authority vouches for is refused.
connections.firstTestNote: The first test trusts whatever answers at this address and pins it. Compare the fingerprint with the one the device shows.
connections.testOff: Turn the connection on to test it.
connections.errSecretMoved: Enter the secret again: the address changed.

sso.title: Signing you in
sso.working: Checking the answer from your identity provider…
sso.idpError: Your identity provider did not sign you in ({{error}}). Try again from the sign-in page; if it keeps happening, ask an administrator.
sso.missing: This page needs the answer from your identity provider. Start again from the sign-in page.

updates.meta: This is a container-only install on your own Docker or Podman, without the helper vedette-host, so you update Vedette and this machine yourself.
updates.title: Update Vedette
updates.desc: Vedette looks for a new release by itself and says so here. You update it on the machine that runs it: keep the files you run now, download the four files of the new release and check their signatures, then pull the new images and start them.
updates.label: In the folder of compose.yaml
updates.again: These two commands pull again the images that vedette.env names (the release you run) and start them, for example after you change a line of vedette.env. They do not move you to a new release: the image digests are fixed in vedette.env. When a release is offered, this page shows its steps; they are also in docs/INSTALL-CONTAINER.md section 5. If you run the sensors or syslog too, add {{files}} after --env-file vedette.env in both commands (leave out the add-on you do not run).
updates.offer: Vedette {{version}} is available. This machine runs {{running}}.
updates.offerUnknown: Vedette {{version}} is available. This machine's version is not known.
updates.checkOff: The update check is off, so Vedette cannot tell you here when a new release is out. Watch the release page, or turn the check on under
updates.notYet: No release information yet: no update check has run on this install. Vedette checks a few minutes after setup or a restart, then every 6 hours.
updates.notYetFailed: No release information yet: no update check has succeeded on this install. Vedette tries again every 6 hours.
updates.latest: No newer release is offered to this install.
updates.runningUnknown: This machine's version is not known.
updates.unsafe: The version offered ({{version}}) or the version this machine runs ({{running}}) cannot be put into a command as it is, so no commands are shown here. Follow docs/INSTALL-CONTAINER.md section 5 by hand.
updates.unsafeUnknown: This machine's version is not known, so no commands are shown here. Follow docs/INSTALL-CONTAINER.md section 5 by hand.
updates.stepKeep: In the folder of compose.yaml, move the four files you run now into a new folder {{kept}}, named after the version they run: that is the way back. An update replaces all four; your own settings are the two lines of vedette.env. mkdir refuses a folder that is already there, so nothing kept is overwritten.
updates.keptThere: If {{kept}} is already there (an update you stopped, or a way back you took), first put its files back, then rename it, and run this step again:
updates.keepLabel: Keep the files you run now
updates.stepFetch: Download the four files of Vedette {{version}} and their signatures from its release page into this folder. The loop stops at the first file that fails:
updates.stepVerify: Check each one with the vedette.pub you kept from the install (in this folder, not one taken from the release page). The signed comment of each file must name that file and version {{version}}: every line must print "<file> ok". At the first FAILED, stop:
updates.matchLabel: Check that vedette.env names these images
updates.pullLabel: Pull the new images and start them
updates.failStop: If any check fails, stop and put your files back.
updates.backOffer: Putting your files back is also the way back after the update. If you run the sensors or syslog too, add {{files}} after --env-file vedette.env (leave out the add-on you do not run). A version that changes the database may not go back: read the release notes and back up first.
updates.backLabel: Put the files of {{kept}} back and start them
updates.verifyWhy: Check that each image of {{version}} is the one the Vedette project signed, with the cosign.pub you kept from the install:
updates.verifyLabel: One line per image, by the digest in the signed release information
updates.matchWhy_one: Check that the new vedette.env names this image; it must print {{count}}, or do not go on:
updates.matchWhy_other: Check that the new vedette.env names these same images; it must print {{count}}, or do not go on:
updates.stepLines: Copy your two lines VEDETTE_BIND_IP and VEDETTE_HOSTS from {{kept}}/vedette.env into the new vedette.env (a release leaves them empty), then pull the new images and start them. If you run the sensors or syslog too, add {{files}} after --env-file vedette.env in both commands (leave out the add-on you do not run):

os.title: Operating system
os.desc: Update the operating system of this machine yourself, with its own tools; Vedette only updates its own images here.

data.meta: Export, log downloads and deleting the data work from here. A backup of this container-only install is a copy of its Docker volume, made on the machine that runs it.

backup.title: Backup
backup.desc: Everything Vedette keeps, the key that unlocks its secrets included, is in the Docker or Podman volume vedette_data. Copy it with core stopped.
backup.label: Back up (in the folder of compose.yaml)
backup.keep: vedette-data.tgz holds the key: keep it as safe as a password. The sensors' creds-passive and creds-active volumes need no backup: core writes them again from vedette_data at every start.
backup.podmanNote: On a machine with SELinux (Fedora, RHEL), add :Z to the "$PWD":/backup mount of the backup command and :ro,Z to the same mount of the restore command.

network.meta: This is a container-only install: the network of this machine is yours to set up.
network.title: Network of this machine
network.desc: Prepare the SPAN card on this machine yourself (promiscuous, no address), start the sensor with compose.sensors.yaml, then choose the card under Sensors. The address, extra IP and time server of the machine are set with its own tools.
network.descNoSpan: Start the sensor with compose.sensors.yaml, then choose the card it listens on under Sensors. The address, extra IP and time server of the machine are set with its own tools.
